key_insight: In India’s eSanjeevani telemedicine service, both hub clinicians and spoke providers generally accepted AI clinical decision support, but acceptance varied when the AI output felt inaccurate, incomplete, or poorly calibrated to the case.
clinical_relevance: AI decision support was viewed as useful for triage and review workflows, but its real-world value depends on reliable symptom capture, relevant questions, and actionable diagnostic suggestions.
method: Program feedback web survey of hub clinicians and spoke providers in eSanjeevani
Compared acceptance and difficulty patterns within each role using absolute differences with Newcombe 95% CIs
Included short open-ended comments analyzed for recurring themes
evidence_signal: Survey data from 190 hub and 662 spoke respondents across 13 and 15 Indian states showed high intention to continue use, with lower acceptance when suggestions were mostly inappropriate or absent.
watch_item: The findings come from a short voluntary feedback survey, so results may reflect response bias and may not capture longer-term workflow effects or patient outcomes.
paper_title: Provider Experiences with AI Clinical Decision Support in eSanjeevani
